title: Class-wise Balancing Data Replay for Federated Class-Incremental Learning

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 states that heterogeneity (β) for CIFAR10 is only 0.5/1.0, but both Table 2 and Table 3 include a column labeled 'CIFAR10 β=0.1' with numerical results. This contradicts the experimental settings described earlier.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 (TinyImageNet β=0.1 column) and Table 3 (TinyImageNet β=0.1 column)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: In Table 2 the column for TinyImageNet β=0.1 contains a value only for FedCBDR (18.35±1.0), while all baseline rows are blank; in Table 3 the same column is completely empty for every method. This makes the comparison incomplete and the tables misleading.

The text states 'class 79 is missing in Task 4 under Re-Fed.' With CIFAR100 split into 5 tasks, Task 4 covers classes 80–99, so class 79 belongs to Task 3, not Task 4. The claim does not match the task structure.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 vs. Table 4 (TinyImageNet β=0.1 results for FedCBDR/GDR+TTS)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 2 reports FedCBDR on TinyImageNet β=0.1 as 18.35±1.0, while the ablation in Table 4 lists GDR+TTS (i.e., full FedCBDR) on the same setting as 18.37±1.1. The values differ beyond plausible rounding.

predicted_errors.error_location: Equation (6) and the 'Global Sampling Procedure' text in Section 4.1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The probability is defined per client as p_k^{i,j} = τ_k^{i,j} / ∑_{j'} τ_k^{i,j'}, which sums to 1 within each client. The text then says to perform i.i.d. sampling based on the set p = {p_k^{i,j}} across all clients, which does not sum to 1 and is therefore not a valid probability distribution (sums to K). This breaks the sampling procedure unless a global re-normalization is implied but not stated.

For 100 samples and feature dimension 512 (float32), the upload per client should be ~0.2 MB, not 3.906 MB. 100 samples × 512 floats × 4 bytes = 204,800 bytes = 0.195 MB. The reported 3.906 MB is an order of magnitude too large, indicating a calculation error.
